In defence of the penguins

By: Johann Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
May one wrong decision mean the extinction of the only penguin species found in africa?

Unique Selling Point:
Lots of cute footage of penguins :) And some serious questions asked of the conservation body that has to save them from extinction.

Summary:
Population numbers of the african penguin has dropped by 90% over the past 60 years and the figures still keep on declining. Many scientists reckon we may already have reached the tipping point where the species is caught in "the extinction curve". Currently the worldwide figures stand at 19000 breeding pairs in South Africa and another 4000 estimated in namibia. All of the breeding colonies have been declining for years except one - Stony Point in betts Bay. This colony accounts for about 13% of the total population. The penguins arrived here in the 1980's and started breeding on the edge of this stony outcrop, and as their numbers increased they slowly also started breeding on the 11 residential properties on Stony Point. The local municipality started managing the colony as a tourist attraction, but no real conservation work was done. As other colonies started collapsing Stony Point suddenly found itself being the most important breeding colony for this enigmatic species and Overstrand municipality started handing over the control to the provincial conservation body, Cape nature. During the process of handing over, the tourism facilities were upgraded, and it was also decided to fence the edge of stony point off from the residential properties protect the penguins from disturbances and threats by residents, their dogs, and also the otters and even a caracal that seemed to prey on the penguins. However, no official study was done on the impact the fence would have on this crucial breeding colony - although at the time only about 300 pairs nested between the houses, the properties represent almost 2/3's of the habitat available for the expanding colony. The fence was erected in Dec 2012, and now we revisit the colony to see what impact the fence has had - and how the colony is doing.

2 flights to cape town from jhb

3 month old penguin chick

Press Release:


African Penguin in Danger
African Penguin population numbers have dropped by a staggering 98 percent over the past 80 years and remain on the decline. Some scientists are of the opinion that the species may already be caught up in the extinction curve and that significant efforts need to be made to secure existing colonies while interventions are sought. Carte Blanche asks: is the most important breeding colony that’s left being managed appropriately? Or is the approach to its protection simply courting the further demise of this penguin?


Script:


Penguin final

New Script 27/08



This baby penguin has been separated from its mother. It’s stuck on the wrong side of this fence. Her nest is between the fence and the base of this cell phone tower inside the conservation area on Stony Point in Betty's Bay. During the day he hides in the bush next to the fence. Everyday his parents still feed him. But our day/night camera shows he is not alone. A few adult escapees, also living on the outside of the fence, regularly check in on him. We don't yet fully comprehend the intricate social interactions that take place among penguins. If the authorities spot the baby, he will likely be sent to a rehab centre. Of the 286 so-called ‘abandoned chicks’ removed from the colony in 2015, 39 died.
Graphic Google Earth
Stony Point is a part of the Western Cape village of Betty's Bay. It used to be a whaling station where penguins were often burnt alive to fuel the massive blubber pots. Thankfully that stopped in 1930.


Google Earth again
The penguinss arrived and started breeding at Stony Point in the 1980s. 20 years later it had grown to the extent that birds–-to the delight of some and irritation of others—were nesting in virtually every garden belonging to the dozen or so unfenced holiday homes on the Point. But the birds were in trouble. By the early 2000s the conservation world woke up to the fact that the species was caught up in the extinction curve. Their numbers had plummeted by 98 percent in just 80 years. Suddenly this colony became very important.
John Link
Today there are 27 breeding colonies left, and ironically the one here at Stony Point is the only one showing positive population growth. The others, sadly, are on their way out...

By 2013, a biodiversity plan was gazetted for the now officially “endangered” penguins with the objective to halt their downward spiral by 2015. This objective failed, and now, 3 years later, only 19 000 breeding pairs remain--another 1000 pairs down from when the plan was first implemented. Cape Nature took over management of the Stony point colony. Claiming the penguins needed protection from the residents, they recommended fencing the penguins in all along the edge of the point on the border of the municipal land—even though the colony was doing well without a fence. Cormac Cullinan is an environmental lawyer and also author of Wild Law.
Cormac
I think they come from a paradigm where they are told that your job is to protect these particular areas, to protect them from outside threats, etcetera, and to control particular areas of land. So it's embedded in the way of thinking. The trouble is we can't protect the earth by creating a series of arks, where we have little boats where we put on a few protected species, while everything else gets destroyed.

Cormack’s modern way of thinking about conservation is one that well-known ecologist and bird man Dr Gerhard Verdoorn agrees with.
Gerhard
Well, globally there is a tendency to move away from fencing because we all know, the moment you put up a fence, you restrict the wildlife, and we've seen all over the world where they put up fencing it has a massive impact on animals that move over land, ungulates, birds, that type of stuff like this, so fencing is a no-go if you're talking about real conservation.

They would argue that other options should have first been pursued.
Cormack
One of the ways, obviously would be to get the people in the area to accept that penguins are africans too – they are an indigenous species more than we are. They have an absolute right to be there, and we can live together.
V/o
Cape Nature also ignored the cautionary principle: first carry out a study to determine the impact of such a drastic move on the colony.



V/o
In courtship, the male penguin presents the female with a pebble and once she accepts, they mate for life. They also return to the same nesting spot every year.
For the penguins on the residential side, the arrival of the fence was traumatic. Apart from the disturbance the work on the fence caused, penguins returning from the sea were suddenly cut off from their nests, their partners and their chicks. Others got trapped on the residential side and couldn't get to the ocean. The fence effectively separated the core colony from fringe members. More than 300 penguins were captured and thrown over the fence, but every night they kept congregating on the old pathways trying to figure out how to get back to where they want to be. Their behaviour clearly showed that the birds were under a lot of stress.


Link John
Habitat is one of the crucial needs of the penguins. When their guano was stripped from the islands they started dying – because their feathers need to be waterproof in the cold southern oceans, and being out of the water is like sitting in the sun with your wetsuit on.
V/o
To counter penguins going into heat stress, tons of cut plant material are continually brought in as shelter, a practice that is likely not sustainable, and which also causes unwanted disturbance to the colony. 2015 data showed 480 abandoned nests on coastal side of the fence. The dead plant material also poses a fire risk.

But according to Cape Nature's Executive director of Conservation management they’re caught between the proverbial fence and the deep blue sea. A fire could wipe out the entire colony but not putting the brush in would definitely result in heat-related fatalities.
Gail
Obviously fire is a threat to the colony. So, the risk assessment has been done and it is a minimal risk using the material. I think the bigger gains that are gotten from using shelter for and protection again, that shelter is very important – using that as a species is fine. And as I say, we have done a risk assessment.
V/o
In 2015 the fynbos on the mountain caught alight. The wind blew the fire through the town and came so close to Stony Point that some of the houses were evacuated. The colony survived...this time....

The fence has also led to a higher population density on the conservation side. Dr Lauren Waller says they are monitoring the health risks this poses.
Lauren
That is one of the things that could potentially be a problem, in any animal species, the higher the density, the more the parasites, so we initiated a project on that.
V/o
Against the mounting odds, the fragile colony is growing. But some say its growth would have been far better had the penguins been left alone. Still, Cape Nature insists that the fence was the best decision.
John Link
The data shows that of the roughly 600 penguins that died in the total colony in 2015 around 200 were killed via caracal in the residential area. And that's CapeNature's main justification of the fence – to safeguard the penguins.
Lauren
And in terms of our breeding success monitoring up to, close to 70% of the nests failed, of birds and nests that were in the residential area.
V/o
But, in any colony predation is always higher around the fringes. What Lauren didn't mention is that according to their 2011 data, after the fence was put up penguin mortalities doubled in the residential area. For many, this is proof enough that the fence might contribute to the many penguin deaths on the outside.

Adding fuel to the controversy is the fact that the fence—erected to keep the penguins out of the residential area—doesn't do that either.

And, in a shock move, Cape Nature's director of conservation announced that they have already put out a tender to replace the current 1.2m fence with an even higher one with a concrete foundation, before the year’s end and to prevent the striped-suit inmates from escaping.
Gail,
And then ultimately being able to protect them. So, we are going to try as far as we can to contain the movement out of the protected area so that we can try and keep them contained.

And while Cape Nature seems set in their ways, the Biosphere Reserve of which Stony forms part, most of the residents we spoke to, many conservationists and of course the penguins, all seem to ask for a new deal, before we lose this very special species, for good...

Cormac
If you look at the Berlin wall, walls we build all over the place, they almost always don't work. The idea of building a barrier that you can't get through is amicable to the idea of relatedness and relationship. It is trying to keep the other out instead of engaging with it.
V/o
Cape Nature claims that the survival of the species is so critical that every bird counts. But while the management debate rages, the little penguin chick is still hiding under a bush, trapped outside the fence. Soon he will have to figure out how to get to the ocean; hopefully one of his older neighbours will show him the long way around the fence.



10 sec Promo
We've lost 98% of Africa's only indigenous penguins in just 80 years. Some say it may already be too late to save them...


15 sec Promo
V/o: Government seems serious about saving our penguins from extinction
Upsound: So, we are going to try as far as we can to contain the movement out of the protected area
V/o: But are they on the right track?



15 sec Promo
V/o: The African Penguin is on the brink of extinction...

Upsound: To protect them we need to contain them.

V/o: Who knows what is best for them? Cape Nature or those calling for drastic new solutions?

During the process of handing over, the tourism facilities were upgraded, and it was also decided to fence the edge of stony point off from the residential properties protect the penguins from disturbances and threats by residents, their dogs, and also the otters and even a caracal that seemed to prey on the penguins. However, no official study was done on the impact the fence would have on this crucial breeding colony - although at the time only about 300 pairs nested between the houses, the properties represent almost 2/3's of the habitat available for the expanding colony. The fence was erected in Dec 2012, and now we revisit the colony to see what impact the fence has had - and how the colony is doing.
